title: Joining tables with merge
setup:
import pandas as pd
games = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
studios = pd.read_csv("studios.csv")
explanation: Welcome to Level 4! Real data is often split across tables. The games table has a studio_id, but the studio's name and country live in a separate studios table. merge() glues two tables together side by side, matching rows on a shared column: games.merge(studios, on="studio_id"). This lesson has two tables ready for you, called games and studios (not df). It's the same idea as JOIN in SQL.

lines.explain: Line up each game with the studio that has the same studio_id.
Show just the game title and studio name.

tasks.prompt: Predict first: how many rows will the merged table have? (games has 15 rows, studios has 12.)
hints: Each game finds exactly one studio.
You get one row per matching game.

solution_lines.explain: Each of the 15 games matches one studio, so 15 rows. Studios with no games (Valve, Ubisoft) are left out by default.

tasks.prompt: Fill in the blank to merge games and studios on studio_id.
hints: Which word tells merge() the shared column?

solution_lines.explain: on= names the column both tables share.

tasks.prompt: Show every game's title next to the name of the studio that made it.
Show the title and studio_name of games made by studios from Japan.
hints: Merge into a variable, say m. Then filter on the country column, which came from studios.

solution_lines.explain: Store the merged table in m.

tasks.prompt: Show the average game price for each studio country, rounded to 2 decimals.

recap: You just learned to join tables with merge(on=...), so information from different tables can be analysed together.
